source.title: CLIP-D ISSECT : A UTOMATIC D ESCRIPTION OF N EU - RON R EPRESENTATIONS IN D EEP V ISION N ETWORKS

page_placements.theme: Many units in other domains and architectures lack a single-concept description
What units encode, and how polysemantic or describable they are, varies with depth (vision and audio classifiers; LM neuron roles in the original SoLU source)

record.tranche_reason: The study measures how well neuron descriptions match activations, and explicitly reports that descriptions become less representative over wider activation ranges and that some neurons may have different functions at different ranges. This refines how neuron interpretability should be assessed; it does not directly count polysemantic neurons.
record.gate_note: The study evaluates neuron-description quality and how it changes with activation range and scoring. It does not directly measure whether individual neurons respond to several unrelated features, or test the specific InceptionV1 neuron in the claim. Table 1–4 results compare description methods or their efficiency and do not measure the claim's object. Figure 1 and other qualitative examples do not provide a direct count of unrelated feature mixtures.
record.test_reason: This is a neuron-labeling method paper. Its numbers score how well CLIP-Dissect descriptions match top-activating images, which measures the method's quality, not whether neurons respond to unrelated inputs. Its only relevant result is a qualitative aside (A.7): on selected most-interpretable neurons, images from the top 1% and top 5% of activations show concepts only slightly related to the description. It never classifies neurons as polysemantic or monosemantic. It neither tests nor relies on any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The main conclusion is that CLIP-Dissect labels hidden neurons more accurately and much faster than NetDissect and MILAN, and that neurons joined by high weights encode similar concepts. The remark that some neurons have complicated functions or different functions at different activation ranges is a stated limitation, not a tested finding.
record.recipe_differences: Uses CLIP-based concept descriptions, activation-range sampling, and human judgments of description match; it does not use the original sources’ methods for identifying or interpreting circuits or features.
record.method_sensitivity: The activation range examined changes how well descriptions match: the top 0.1% generally matches, while the top 1% and 5% include different, slightly related concepts. Description scores also vary by layer.

fits_no_version.finding: For the most interpretable neurons, descriptions match images in the top 0.1% of activations. Images in the top 1% and 5% show concepts only slightly related to the description. Low-level concepts such as colours stay more consistent across ranges (qualitative, Figs 12–13).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Automated neuron descriptions fitted to top activations lose fidelity at wider activation ranges, more so for high-level concepts.

fits_no_version.finding: Using a SoftWPMI cutoff, 69.7% (ResNet-18) and 77.8% (ResNet-50) of neurons count as interpretable, implying about 20–30% have no simple single-concept description.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A sizeable minority of CNN neurons lack a simple single-concept description under CLIP-based labeling.

fits_no_version.finding: Description match is highest in conv1 and layer4 and lower in middle layers, in both the expert ratings and the MTurk ratings.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Single-concept describability of CNN neurons varies by depth, with middle layers hardest to describe.

record.problems: Description matching is subjective: the authors report 68.4% agreement between two evaluators in Appendix A.10 and note noise in the crowdsourced ratings. The activation-range evidence is qualitative and covers selected most-interpretable neurons in two models; the paper does not directly measure the frequency of unrelated feature mixtures.
record.rows_left_out: Qualitative neuron-label examples in Figure 1 and Appendices A.2–A.5 were not recorded as separate rows because they do not report a direct activation-range comparison or measure whether a neuron has unrelated functions. The figures in A.7 are represented by the textual aggregate descriptions rather than individual figure-only neuron examples.

untested.parts: No neuron is shown or counted as responding to several unrelated inputs; InceptionV1 is not studied.
Initialization, regularization and training noise are not examined.
No comparison of activation functions or architectures for polysemanticity; ViT results are qualitative only.
Canonical polysemantic neurons are not revisited.
No polysemanticity classification is made at different activation ranges or under different scorings. Only qualitative description drift is reported, on selected neurons.

record.verdict_notes: This is a method paper. The reader's 'tests/T5' with V7 labels overreads a qualitative appendix aside. The rows are the method's own performance numbers, so all are relinked to none and no verdicts are given.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test whether neurons respond to several unrelated inputs, nor the stated InceptionV1 example.
No language models or transformer MLP neurons are studied.
The study does not test superposition or capacity pressure as a cause.
The study does not test initialization, regularization, or training noise as causes.
It does not compare activation functions or test whether polysemanticity can be reduced without performance loss.
The study does not revisit canonical polysemantic neurons to establish that their apparently unrelated inputs share one feature.

Tests changes in description match across activation ranges and layers, and reports results under its own explanation-scoring procedures. It does not compare multiple formal polysemanticity metrics or determine whether the differing inputs share a feature the network uses.

rows.subject: ResNet-18 and ResNet-50
rows.stage_stated: ResNet-18 trained on Places-365; ResNet-50 trained on ImageNet
rows.operation_detail: Rated neurons using descriptions randomly selected from the concept set.
rows.baseline: CLIP-Dissect descriptions: average 3.57 across both models and layers
rows.note: The authors call this a baseline/sanity test and note that its score is still higher than expected, indicating noise in the crowdsourced evaluations.
rows.check: A sanity check comparing random descriptions with the method's descriptions. It validates the method and says nothing about polysemanticity.

rows.subject: ResNet-18
rows.operation_detail: Classified neurons as interpretable when the description similarity exceeded τ = 0.16.
rows.measure: Share of neurons classified as interpretable
rows.note: The authors define this result through their description-similarity cutoff; it is not a direct count of polysemantic neurons.
rows.check: Share of neurons above a SoftWPMI cutoff that the authors tuned on their own evaluation. Being uninterpretable is not the same as responding to unrelated features.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

relation.reason: Discusses neurons with complicated functions or different functions at different activation ranges (Limitations, A.7) but does not test or use the claim. A.8's uninterpretable share is defined by a cutoff and is not a polysemanticity measure.

tranche.reason: A neuron-labeling method paper whose scores measure how good its descriptions are. The paper never uses the word polysemantic. A.7 (activation-range figures) and the Limitations remark are qualitative and not a test of any version.

source_check.notes: A.7 shows only in figures, on hand-picked most-interpretable neurons, that top-1%/5% images drift to 'only slightly related' concepts. The authors partly blame the probe set. This bears loosely on V7 but is not a test. B.2 has a random-description baseline of 2.61, pooled over all layers, not per layer. The 'all five layers' scope of r22/r23 is inferred: A.8 does not name the layers.

statements.correction: A.8: with SoftWPMI cutoff tau=0.16 (picked using the A.10 ratings), 69.7% of ResNet-18 (Places-365) and 77.8% of ResNet-50 (ImageNet) neurons count as interpretable.

A.10: two evaluators (background not stated), 50 random neurons per layer, yes/maybe/no. B.2: MTurk, 3 raters per neuron, up to 200 neurons per layer, 1-5 scale. conv1 and layer4 rank top two in each case. ResNet-50 layer4 only just beats layer1 (0.695 vs 0.670; 3.50 vs 3.48).
statements.problem: The ranking is right for both models in both ratings, but the text never calls the A.10 raters experts. It only says 'our two evaluators'.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Top activation ranges in the illustrated ResNet-18 and ResNet-50 neurons
reader_labels.reason: Descriptions match well for the top 0.1% of activations, while the top 1% and 5% include quite different, only slightly related concepts (r24–r29), showing that the assessment changes with the activation range examined.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Description scoring across the five layers of ResNet-18 and ResNet-50
reader_labels.reason: Description scores vary by layer, and the authors’ cutoff classifies 69.7% and 77.8% of neurons as interpretable (r1–r10, r22–r23); these scoring-based rates do not establish how many neurons truly have unrelated functions.
